opis: Feeling unfulfilled is not a flaw in your faith. Longing as something God built into us on purpose.
zdanie: Feeling unfulfilled is not a defect of faith. It is evidence that we were made for something greater than what we have.

elementy.tekst: Longing is not sadness. Sadness is about what has been lost; longing is about what isn’t here yet. The Bible treats it not as a lack of faith or as ingratitude, but as something built into human beings on purpose. This meeting aims to lift from people the feeling that being unfulfilled is a spiritual defect.
**Where the landmines are:**

pozycje: Someone may be longing for a person who has died or who never came back. A text about longing for God may then sound like a reproach.
Philippians 1 speaks of a desire to depart. With someone who has attempted suicide or who is depressed, handle it carefully.
Don’t turn this meeting into a conversation about heaven as a reward. The point is how longing works, not a description of eternity.

elementy.tekst: **What not to do:** don’t tell anyone they should long more for God and less for earthly things. Don’t compete over whose desires are more spiritual.
What did you long for as a child so intensely that you still remember it today? One sentence.
answer first, and pick something ordinary.

akapity: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?

elementy.tekst: The psalmist compares himself to an animal looking for water. **What does that comparison say about the nature of his longing: is it a desire for pleasure, or for something else?**
He asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” **Doesn’t he believe God is everywhere? What is he after?**
A few verses later the same psalm says, “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” **How does longing sit next to sadness here?**

The deer doesn’t pant for water because it is ungrateful for what it has. It pants because without water it dies. The psalmist chooses an image from the realm of needs, not whims. His question about appearing in God’s presence is not doubt about God being present. It is longing for a presence he can feel, the way he did at the temple, among people and song. In the Bible, longing for God is often very concrete and tied to a place.

akapity: How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts! My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God. … For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked.

elementy.tekst: The psalm opens with “How lovely is Your dwelling place,” and then says the soul longs, even faints. **How can longing hurt and delight at the same time?**
Verse 10 does the math: one day is worth more than a thousand. **What do you have to live through to make a calculation like that?**
He would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell anywhere else. **A doorkeeper stands at the threshold, not in the center. What is he choosing?**

akapity: O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water. So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory. Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You.

elementy.tekst: Here it is not only the soul that longs, but the body too. **What does that image add?**
“Your loving devotion is better than life.” **That sentence puts something above life itself. Can anyone say it honestly?**

akapity: We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. For in this hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see? But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.

elementy.tekst: Paul says it is not only the world that groans, but also those who already have the Spirit. **Does faith lessen longing, or sharpen it?**
Verse 24: “hope that is seen is no hope at all.” **What does that mean for living with a sense that something is missing?**
Paul links waiting with patience. **What is missing from a longing that has no patience?**

This is one of the few places where Paul describes a Christian as someone who groans. It is not a failure of faith or a stage to get past, but the normal condition between a promise and its fulfillment. What is striking is that, according to Paul, having the Spirit does not put out longing; it strengthens it. A person who has had a taste longs more than someone who doesn’t know what it’s about.

akapity: All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own. If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.

elementy.tekst: These people died without receiving what was promised. **The writer still holds them up as an example. Why?**
They called themselves strangers and exiles. **What does naming it that way do to the feeling of being out of place?**
Verse 15 says they could have gone back if they had wanted to. **How is longing for what lies ahead different from longing for what lies behind?**
“God is not ashamed to be called their God.” **What is that sentence doing here, in the middle of a passage about promises not yet fulfilled?**

akapity: For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labor for me. So what shall I choose? I do not know. I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.

elementy.tekst: Paul says plainly that he doesn’t know what to choose. **Is that being torn apart, or maturity?**
He settles the matter not by what is better for him, but by something else. **By what?**

bloki.tytul: The Last Words of the Bible

akapity: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” Let the one who hears say, “Come!” And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely. … He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

elementy.tekst: The Bible ends with the plea “Come,” not with a description of fulfillment. **What does that say about where it leaves the reader?**
The invitation is addressed to “the one who is thirsty.” **Is thirst a condition here, or simply a way of recognizing who is invited?**
Longing shows what really matters to you. **What absence has bothered you most this year?** Answer yourself honestly, even if the answer isn’t a pious one.
Hebrews 11 speaks of people who died before they saw it. **Is there something you will probably not live to see? How do you live with that?**
If you want to share: **when was the last time you felt, even for a moment, that you weren’t missing anything?**
Feeling unfulfilled is not a defect of faith. It is evidence that we were made for something greater than what we have.
**Verse to remember:** Psalm 42:1 or Hebrews 11:16.
Name your longing specifically. **Not “something is missing,” but what exactly.** Unnamed longing spills over into everything and usually comes back as irritability.
Notice what you most often use to drown out the sense that something is missing: work, screens, food, planning. **Ask God what you are really looking for when you reach for that thing.**
**For the brave:** stay with your longing for one evening without doing anything about it. No drowning it out, and no instantly turning it into a prayer for a solution.

**“We should long for God, not for earthly things.”** It sounds pious, and it shuts the conversation down. Paul longed for people, David for the temple and for a specific place. Don’t separate these too neatly.
**Someone talks about longing for a loved one who has died.** That is exactly the subject, not a detour. Don’t quickly redirect it to longing for God.
**Someone says they wish they could die already.** Don’t quote Philippians 1 to them right away. Calmly ask what they mean, and be sure to follow up with them after the meeting.
**The conversation drifts into the details of life in heaven.** Gently return to the text. This topic is not about eschatology but about what unfulfillment does to a person.
**“I’m not missing anything.”** Don’t confront. Shift it: “Is there anything you’re waiting for?”
**Silence.** Longing is harder to name than anger, because there is no one to blame. Wait longer than usual.
